newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU issues tough warning on Boeing-McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: EU issues tough warning on Boeing-McDonnell merger.

text.p: The European Commission, in its strongest language to date, said on Tuesday it would block a proposed $14 billion merger between Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. unless European antitrust concerns were addressed.

The commission said Boeing had not yet made enough proposals to address its fears that the merger would strengthen Boeing's dominant position and harm fair competition in the EU market for commercial aircraft.
"Boeing has so far not agreed to measures which would meet these concerns," it said.

Only one week before it is expected to make a final ruling on the deal, the commission also formally backed the tough stance taken against the merger by its antitrust chief, Commissioner Karel Van Miert.

"Unless the legitimate competition concerns of the commission can be met and genuine choice maintained for purchasers of aircraft worldwide, the Commission could not approve the merger," commission chief spokesman Nikolaus van der Pas said in a statement that was unprecedented in a merger case.
The statement removed any doubts about the EU's determination to resist warnings from the United States that a ban would cause a damaging political fight between the two trade partners.
Boeing said it still hoped for an agreement despite the commission's latest warning.

"We believe that the proposals put forward (by Boeing) are an honest effort to meet the commission's concerns. I'm hopeful there will be a deal," Jim Frank, Boeing's vice president for European affairs, told Reuters.

Under EU law, the commission has the power to block mergers and takeovers involving companies with a combined worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units ($5.5 billion) and 250 million Ecus ($227.5 million) each in sales within the 15-nation bloc.

If Boeing went ahead with the deal regardless of the decision, the commission could fine it up to 10 percent of revenue and also fine any European companies that did business with it. Commission sources said the EU could also seize any new planes being delivered in Europe.
Antitrust lawyers believe Boeing will not run the risk of being shut of the European market, which accounts for 30 percent of the world's total aircraft orders.

They said that Boeing, which would increase its share of the civilian aircraft market with more than 100 seats to 70 percent from 64 percent and see its customer base jump to 84 percent from 60 percent with the merger, will eventually negotiate, though it may wait until the last minute to do so.
"I believe Boeing will test the commission's patience until July 22," an industry source said, referring to the day before the commission is expected to make its final decision.

The commission had originally given Boeing a deadline of midnight Monday, Brussels time, to alleviate the commission's concerns about the merger's antitrust implications. But when the talks ran on into the night, it pushed the final deadline back a week to July 23.
The commission has expressed concerns about the merger's impact on competition in several areas.

It opposes Boeing's exclusive contracts to supply aircraft to airlines such as Delta Air Lines, American Airlines and Continental Airlines, and worries about the possibility of spillovers of government money, earmarked for research and development in defence, into Boeing's civil aviation business.
Although McDonnell Douglas has become a minor player in the civil aviation sector, the commission is also concerned that the deal will increase Boeing's customer base.

About 25 percent of all planes in the world's fleets are McDonnell's, and the commission fears Boeing will somehow tie the servicing and maintenance of those planes to their replacement by its own aircraft. It also sees McDonnell's spare parts business as a lucrative addition to Boeing's business.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission cleared the deal without conditions earlier this month.
Boeing's stock price rose 94 cents a share to $58.00 on the New York Stock Exchange. McDonnell Douglas gained $1.13 to $73.94, also on the NYSE.
